title: Beyond Autonomous Teams in Software Product Development
gist: At Craft conference, Simon Rohrer argues organizations should replace 'autonomous product team' thinking with 'value center' thinking, using a five-question framework derived from Stafford Beer's Viable Systems Model and a 'simple vs. complex molecule' metaphor to explain why some services decouple cleanly into independent teams while others cannot decouple their value even if the code is split.

themes.theme: From product focus to value-center thinking

insights.claim: In a vaguely complicated organization, what an individual team delivers is rarely a discrete 'product' but part of a value stream that changes every quarter, project, initiative, and feature, which is why thinking in terms of 'products' is the wrong language for describing team value.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: Challenges the common practice of organizing engineering teams around fixed 'product' boundaries; leaders evaluating org design should ask what value stream a team actually sits in, not what product it nominally owns.
insights.locator: opening paragraphs on value center concept

insights.claim: The shape of an organization's value — its web of internal and external dependencies, some accidental and some essential — directly constrains what the organization's structure can look like and how it trades off autonomy against coherence.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: Provides a diagnostic lens for org design: before restructuring into autonomous teams, map the actual dependency shape of the value being delivered, since that shape — not preference — sets the limits.
insights.locator: paragraph on the web of dependencies

themes.theme: Five-question framework from the Viable Systems Model

insights.claim: Rohrer proposes five questions that every 'value center' at every organizational level (individual, team, team-of-teams, department, whole organization) should be able to answer: what value am I delivering, how do we coordinate, how do we fit together, what's out there for us, and who are we — a framework derived from Stafford Beer's 1960s Viable Systems Model in management cybernetics.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: A concrete, portable diagnostic checklist leaders can apply to any team or team-of-teams to assess whether its coordination and boundaries are actually coherent, independent of specific methodology (Scrum, SAFe, etc.).

insights.claim: A system's purpose is defined by what it actually does today, not by what it ought to do or aspires to do, so diagnosing an organization's real purpose requires looking at observed behavior rather than mission statements.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: A practical audit technique: when redesigning team structure, assess purpose from what a team actually produces and does, not its charter — surfaces mismatches that pure org-chart review would miss.
insights.quote: We’re not what we ought to do, not what we think we might do, but we are what we do. That is our purpose today.

themes.theme: Simple vs. complex molecules: when value can and cannot be decoupled

insights.claim: A global public cloud operator like Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure can offer standalone services with minimal dependencies (e.g. a file service like S3 or a compute service like EC2, akin to 'simple molecules'), whereas a trading platform combining pricing, risk analytics, and trading capabilities behaves like a 'complex organic molecule' whose elements only make sense to customers when linked together.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: Gives operators and investors a mental model for judging which business lines can be cleanly split into autonomous teams (or spun off) and which cannot, because the interdependency lives in the value delivered to the customer, not just in the codebase.
insights.quote: You can decouple technically how you develop and deploy these elements, but you can’t decouple their value.
insights.locator: InfoQ interview answer on visualizing value shapes

insights.claim: Rohrer maps his five questions onto existing Scrum ceremonies — 'how do we coordinate' corresponds to the backlog and sprint plan, and 'how do we fit together' corresponds to the sprint goal and Fred Brooks' concept of 'conceptual integrity' — meaning the framework is meant to overlay existing agile practice rather than replace it.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: Teams already running Scrum can apply this framework incrementally as an interpretive lens rather than adopting a wholesale new methodology.
insights.locator: interview answer on 'How do we coordinate?' and 'How do we fit together?'

themes.theme: Order vs. disorder, and moving beyond autonomous teams

insights.claim: Quoting Ralph Stacey, Rohrer frames organizational life as a paradox of intertwined order and disorder, and argues that although most managers are more comfortable with order, today's environment has more disorder than order, making a bias toward coherence more useful than a bias toward pure autonomy.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the default industry preference for maximizing team autonomy; leaders should weight coherence more heavily in environments experiencing high disorder (e.g. rapid AI-driven change).
insights.quote: there’s a lot more disorder than order these days

insights.claim: Rohrer's overall recommendation is to move organizations from autonomous, siloed product teams toward a structure that is 'nested and networked,' where teams do not need to traverse the management hierarchy in order to deliver value together.
insights.speaker: Simon Rohrer
insights.so_what: An implicit critique of the widely-copied 'autonomous squad' (Spotify-style) org model; worth watching whether 'value center' or networked-team framing gains traction as an alternative playbook among engineering leaders.
insights.locator: closing summary paragraph of the talk recap
